p: When a parent proactively seeks preventative services because they're struggling with child behavior challenges, including violence or high-risk behavior, what is the average time between referral and the start of services? Are there differences in wait times based on borough provider or level of need?

There's no wait list. We're able to provide services right away. Sometimes, it does take a few conversations and visits to begin, you know, and engage that work. And so, it can take up to a couple weeks, but that's really based on a family reaching out voluntarily. We don't have any wait list in any part of the city. We've also created this, as I was referencing earlier, this teen priority initiative. When a hospital calls us, sometimes on the weekends, we get calls from the court after a young person's been arrested and the parent can't pick them up. That should not be a foster care entry and, too often, it has been. And so, we're creating this process where

immediately, we can get the family services, work with those systems, not have that child enter foster care, use respite more often, which we're building out. But I really want to emphasize that we need the help of the mental health system. And this should not be the child welfare system's responsibility. A family should not have to have an intrusive model like that. So, we're working with the Office of Mental Health at the State level, asking them if, you know, they're building a number of services coming out of this consent decree. But families should be able to walk in and get the help that they need. And the system is not designed for young people who are struggling the most. Part of the reason we're seeing too many young people in detention. It's part of the reason we saw an increase in teens. We're going to do everything we can to serve those families when they come to our attention. But I think it'd be great to pay as much attention to figuring out ways in which those services are actually accessible, not just through an emergency room. But if you have an ACT team responding to a crisis of a teen, that teen should be eligible for all the services that they need, intensive outpatient, day treatment, whatever

it is that they need in a culturally competent way. And we have a long way to go to do that.

No. I mean, I 100 percent agree. I think that that is probably one of the biggest issues where it's like, it's nowhere else to put it. So, let's just put it with ACS, and we haven't been doing real comprehensive work around the mental health services. And I will say this, young people have been advocating since literally for the last four years. That has been one of the number one things they've been asking me for is jobs and mental health services…
Amen.

And young people have been very clear about this. But for some reason, the adults have not been listening. And so, I agree and want to keep making sure that I'm fighting and pushing that and uplifting that young people say they want more services, mental health services, and they want jobs. But, you know, we're not listening. I actually have a lot more.
Career choice is coming.
You said career choice is coming?
It's here. Sorry. Sorry.

As we discussed at a previous hearing, advocates have worked with the Mayor's Office of Policy and Planning on the concept of the office of family well-being that would strengthen community planning for family's life and invest in grassroots organizations to support families. How could it help reduce racial disparities in ACS involvement to build up the family support capacity of grassroots groups?

I think it's a wonderful idea to have a City entity that's focused solely on family wellness. I think it's important that our child protective specialists have at their fingertips supportive services, talked about FPP, talked about preventive services, lots of other things, that there's not just sort of a binary choice for them about sort of removal or not. And so, I do think some things should be connected to the child protective system or at least very easily accessible, but the more that we can put in a place where

families feel less stigma, I absolutely support that. It is complicated. You know, all the procurement stuff, all the contracting, you have to be a local district of social services, but I see no reason we shouldn't urgently kick off a planning process to look at what an office of family well-being would look like.

Yeah. I mean, I think we definitely need to get to a place of like, what does it look like to support families in a real way, and not always as punitive. I think that, again, under your leadership, there has been a real push around trying to have other mechanisms so, it's not always punitive, but I want to be clear, because of a lot of the harm and what has been done in the past, why would now these same families want to trust and say, okay, I want to have a case. And it's still a lot of work that needs to be done there.
And, Chair, if I… even if we have a perfect system…
Yeah.

If you walk with the power to remove a child, that is fear-inducing, period, right, and so, we have to walk with it with

integrity, and follow the law, and make sure we're doing a job to protect those children, but we also have to acknowledge that that is something that families are not going to want to walk towards.

No. Absolutely not. Why would someone sign up for it? And again, I think also, too, again, I know that it's been this big push to say we want other avenues to get into ACS without having to be punitive, but how are you even doing that rebranding? How are families supposed to know? I know we've talked about this a number of times, but could you talk about some of the work that you guys have done to try to let families know that there has been somewhat of a shift, but still with the understanding of why families would still stay away?

Yeah. I think there's a few things happening here. One is we've really tried to allow, whether it's the Family Enrichment Centers or the Community Partnerships, to develop them outside of ACS branding, or even the non-profits branding, so that they are driving sort of a community visioning process. The Preventive Support Line has proved very successful as well in this regard. We're working to try to get out more

messaging. We worked very hard when we were expanding child care to get out messaging around that. In local communities, we went through both for Promise and other services, went through community-based organizations that families trust. There's also the culture shift at ACS, and if I could give a minute or two to Elvita Dominique, our Director of Equity Strategies, and FDC Saunders, just to talk about some of the ways in which we're creating a culture of anti-racism within ACS as well.

So, good afternoon, Honorable Chair and Honorable Members of the Youth and Family Committee. It is my pleasure today to talk to you about the Office of Equity Strategies. It was established in 2018, and it was moved under my purview, the Office of the First Deputy Commissioner, in 2021 to ensure and broaden agency-wide reach. With that being said, there are three units that comprise our office. One is LGBTQIA-plus Equity Strategies, two is Race Equity Strategies, and three is our new Office of Fatherhood Engagement. We work really hard to support all branches of our agency in their efforts to eliminate disparities and

address disparities and disproportionality that impact the families and children and staff that we serve and work with. Some of the things that we've been really focused on… well, let me say, in four different ways we really, these are the primary ways we engage. So, one is improving policy and practice and advancing equity, two is developing initiatives and strategies that eliminate and address these inequities, three is developing a culture and shifting the culture where family voice and youth and parent voice are elevated and respected, and the fourth one is really creating an inclusive environment for our workforce. With that being said, many of the things that our Commissioner mentioned with regard to the expansion of CARES, the launch of early school supports have been mentioned. But there are other things such as training, and we talked about it a little bit through some of the discussions that was had earlier this morning, but our policy refresh, as you know, we've had a policy on LGBTQIA and the promotion of a safe environment, but it was done in 2012. We know that there is a need for a modernization of those policies and making sure that we include the voice of young people and parents and

families. So, we are very much in tune with making sure that we're elevating parent and youth voice. You might know that we actually created a couple of years ago a family engagement specialist that works with the entire agency. Just recently, we've embedded a parent advisor in the Family Services Division. In addition to that, we have a Parent Advocacy Council that weighs in on policies and different protocols that are currently in place or things that they bring to our attention that they want to discuss and they want to elevate. We also have a Youth Leadership Council that also has a voice in the practice and protocols that are happening at ACS. With that being said, there are so many things that I can talk about, but I really want to give an opportunity to our Executive Director, Elvita Dominique, to really discuss some of the work that she leads.

Thank you so much, FDC. You've been so thorough actually already. I just want to add just a few things. With regard to the race equity work, I think today we spent a lot of time talking about our services and the ways in which we're really trying to embed race

equity into those services. Some of that work has already been highlighted. FDC mentioned it, the Commissioner mentioned it. We're talking about expansion of CARES, expansion of the Family Enrichment Centers, expansion of childcare assistance. All of that we consider a part of our race equity strategy work within ACS. I'll focus a little bit more on what we're doing internally in terms of the culture shift. There's a lot of investment going on in terms of staff training. We have actual trainings developed by ACS, such as understanding and undoing implicit bias that's mandated for ACS staff. This training helps staff identify and mitigate bias. But then we also supplement that with additional trainings that we make available to staff as well, such as undoing racism, which we partner with the People's Institute for Survival and Beyond to help staff address how racism operates in large systems. And then to really further allow them to develop that equity lens, we also provide reflective practice and we also provide healing circles. The reflective practice allows for facilitated spaces so staff can kind of take what they've learned in these trainings and really think

about how they can incorporate it into their work. And the healing circles really allow folks to kind of manage the stress that is really involved in doing this work really well. Further to that, in terms of our internal work, ACS has rolled out a scoring tool for interviews agency-wide and all interviews are required to follow a structured interview process to allow for more fairness in our hiring processes. We also have developed internally again an equity checklist that's a tool for staff that they can use to self-reflect and achieve an equity lens before any interactions or meetings. ACS also has an ACS Racial Equity and Cultural Competence Committee, which was founded in 2006 and is actually very influential in the promotion of race equity at ACS and the development of our office, the Office of Race Equity Strategies. The General Committee of the REECC is open to all staff from every level and every division, as well as representatives from provider agencies and the child welfare advocate community. We also have a robust group of resource groups that are open to all staff that include the African American Heritage Committee, the Latino Heritage Committee, the Pride Alliance, and many others. We've developed

also an agency framework, which really identifies what our overall focus is as an agency, and within that framework really has advancing equity as one of the main purposes, so staff can kind of understand how all of our work really is leading towards this greater goal of success for children, youth, and families. So, we're really looking at how all of these tools can really promote the culture shift that we're looking for as an agency.

Thank you. That was a lot. And I know in the conversation we did talk about the parent advocates, and so I know there's about 150 parent advocates with lived experience to help provide mentorship and advocacy for parents with children currently in the foster care system. Are those parent advocates, are they compensated for that work, and what are the rates for families who receive PEP support compared to, what are the unification rates of families who receive PEP supports compared to those who do not, and does ACS determine which families receive a parent advocate, and how do you ensure that they deploy equitable?

So, regarding the Parents Empowering Parents Program, that's within the foster care agency, the foster care continuum, I lost my voice, sorry. So, they are staff, they are hired by the foster care agency, so yes, they are absolutely compensated, they are full-time staff, they are trained by RISE, but they have other on-boarding training, so they're a modified employee of the foster care agency that they work for. They're embedded in the case planning teams. They're the units. So, each unit is a unit of four case planners and a supervisor, so that's about 40 cases, and ideally they are assigned new cases that have a goal of reunification. So that's how they're kind of assigned. I think you asked a question…
About timing. We don't… yeah, okay.
I got that, right, but you asked something else about the parents that get the parent, the PEP, so.
Yeah. How do you determine the parent advocates, how do you ensure that they are deployed equitably?

So, they're embedded in their unit, and we usually, based on new cases, those cases, or cases that are in need, or if a parent has asked for a parent advocate, they are given. So, the goal is for each unit to have their own parent advocate, so that one advocate isn't spread too thin. In terms of being able to track, like, the permanency rates, we're not able to do that at this time. We have been in conversations with OCFS to create a field and connections, for example, so that we could pull that data to see, like, the time it took that particular case to achieve permanency and if there was a parent advocate, but we don't have a way to track that in connections yet, but we'll continue those conversations, and we're hoping, that's definitely data we want to look at.

Yeah. And also, how can we use that in other spaces, right? I think it's important to people who have those experiences to be there to support. Beyond the work that you've talked about, ACS will continue to reduce racial disparities with child welfare. Are there external factors that other

agencies or other agencies should address to support these efforts?

Yeah. I think we've talked about a few of them. I think one of the things is that the child welfare system by law and by responsibility has been imbued with this urgency. That's not necessarily the case in other systems that are helping systems, and so we want to make sure there's as much urgency to get families help to mitigate risk, to provide that kind of help. I think we talked about that, whether that's the mental health system, we're really grateful for the colleagues who have engaged with us around this, both in the mental health system and the hospital system, shelter schools, etc.
Thank you. I'm going to move on to the legislation. I know you've already said that you love the legislation that I'm putting forward. That's what I heard.
Sort of.

And Intro. 449 and Intro. 446 would require ACS representatives to inform parents or guardians that they are not

required to consent to a home visit, search, or speak to ACS staff. Does ACS anticipate that providing this advancement could affect the levels of voluntary cooperation for families?

It could. But let me back up, if I may. A couple years ago, we began providing families with information at the front door about key rights. We share with them that we're there as a result of a call alleging maltreatment. We share with them that we are seeking permission to come in, that they can deny that permission, that if they deny that permission, we have to find the best way to assess the safety of their children, which may include seeking permission from a family court. We also let them know they can call an attorney at any time during the investigation, and we have a packet for them with attorney information in it. That has not changed the rate of which we've been able to carry out assessments and work with families within their home. The legislation, so I think that's really important. We're the only place in the state that is doing this, one of the few places in the country. Some of the additional expectations in the legislation, we're

interested about. I am concerned that given that about 7 percent of families go to court, and that moment of starting the investigation is not consistent with custodial interrogation or arrest, which is when Miranda's ran in law enforcement, that we could, in using that language, actually strike more fear that we are further along. We don't know what would happen to family court. Family court is accessible 24/7. I have a hypothesis that it would increase the number of times we have to seek for an order to produce or an entry order. The current State law and regulation requires that we make an attempt before we seek court intervention, and so that could create challenges in assessing child safety. My view, again, is that we sort of have to narrow the ubiquity of our system but be able to assess child safety when children truly may be in danger, and to make sure we're protecting so, we really hope to continue this conversation about exactly what to say at that front door.

No, I mean, I agree. Listen. My guiding star is always to keep young people safe and children safe, and so that's always my guiding star, but we want to make sure that

parents know their rights and understand their rights, right? And I also believe if you're already doing it, I'm all about codifying, because as we can see, there can be someone at the head that's really good, but they don't stay, so we have to codify the things that we believe are necessary so that when the next person come in, that that policy can't change. And so, I'm very open to amending this and hearing feedback, but I do think that it is important for us to figure out what makes the most sense, especially because you're already testifying that this is something that's already being done to families. My next question is, if a parent refuses entry to ACS, how would Intro. 449 change ACS process for assessing imminent danger during the initial contact?

We're not sure. The current practice that we are pursuing has not changed that. We have staff on all through the night. The court is available, so if we do need to get an entry order, we work to pursue that. Sometimes that escalates things further than might be necessary, so I do worry about unnecessary court involvement, but I

don't want to suggest that we have experience with what that would do.
My next question is, does ACS have data on the number of families where the parents or legal guardians of children who are subject to investigation have limited English proficiency?

We do. 12,383 parents in investigations had a primary language other than English, and we fulfilled 146,441 requests for interpretation. This includes for Child Protective, Families in Prevention, and Foster Care, as well as the Children's Center.
And what does those interpretation services typically consist of?
They consist of Language Line, where there's an on-the-phone…
Yeah. I heard Language Line is terrible.
We've had…
That's what folks have complained to me about.
Say it again. I'm sorry.
Folks have complained about Language Line in a number of ways, and so, you know.

We have new contracts going into place. This is something that it'll be the first time ACS has our own contracts. I think we've seen a lot of success with them, but I'd love to hear any of the concerns. Yeah. They have in-person, which we typically use for conferences and other kinds of.

And Intro. 424 would require DOHMH to establish an operative pilot program to provide mental health services at no cost to children who have been returned to their families following removal by ACS. Approximately, how many children are returned home following an Article X removal each year and what percentages receive mental health services? And my question is, it was my understanding that when young people are transitioning out, there's typically a transition plan, and there's usually services that's already provided. So is this something… I'm trying to figure out what gap we're trying to fill here.

There's two things going on here. One is families who are unifying. Many of those children are much younger, and we have the capacity to continue to serve them for up to a year. Some families want that, some families don't. We do not have the capacity to track what services that they access for some good reasons, HIPAA laws and otherwise, but it would be helpful if we could get more data from OCFS, maybe de-identified from OCFS about children in foster care and the Office of Mental Health as well, just to be able to see how much treatment is being provided. Agencies have all built Article 29Is where they can provide that treatment, both medical and mental health. For young people who are aging out of care, which is a little less than 400 each year, there is, as you know, the coach, there's mental health services that they can attach to. They've also… DC Mendez can talk for a second about, because I know she would love to, about Soul Care. This is something that young people created.
Oh, yes. I remember this. You told me about this in a hearing before.

Yes. So, Soul Care is a public-private partnership we have with Public Policy Lab and a wellness collective, Melody Santana was part of that, and we're really looking at how to provide alternate supports, therapeutic supports, but not your traditional therapy. Because many of our young people have done the CBT, they've done the didactic training.

They said they don't want it. Listen, I hear the kids. That's why I keep saying young people need to be in these spaces, because we keep coming up with things they're like, nah, that's not what we asked for.

So, Soul Care is a small pilot, but we are going to continue moving forward, and so we're able to offer boxing, there's hip hop therapy, there's other things. We're working with an organization called Art Pharmacy. So, we really are trying to support young people to, you know, reach their best potential, but also support them in ways that they want to be supported. And so, we have some funding, we're in the process of trying to expand the pilot, and then we'll probably try to

look at how we can make sure this is baselined and offered.
Is that one of your new needs this year? Because it is budget season.
It will be. We're not there yet, but it will be, yes. I think we're going to probably do that. We need to get the evaluation as well, just to make sure it's effective and continue it.
It's music to my ears when you say you're doing a pilot and an evaluation, because government doesn't do that apparently so, I appreciate that.
So, yeah. So, we're going to try to see, but we really are hearing good things from the pilot.

I just have one more question before I wrap up. ACS testified that children can continue Medicare services up to one year after discharge from foster care agencies notifying the management care company. Even with the Medicare eligibility, are there provider shortages or long wait lists that prevents timely access to care?

Because that was something that we heard from young people from some of the roundtables we've done.

For this particular population, they are able to access it ongoing through the same care that they've been receiving while they're in care, but yes, there are absolute needs for greater mental health access in the community.

Yeah. That was one of the things that we were hearing, that even when they do have a plan and have Medicare, there's still long wait lists or limited options, and so, that is definitely something we will be working with Chair Cabán on to figure out how do we continue to do the expanded services.

There is a pilot that we're doing with Northwell, for young people who are interested in being part of their Healthy Home Continuum and accessing services, we gave them stipends to learn more about it and just to see if there's a way to create a health community for them. So, something else that we might be learning from in the future.

Well, with that, I don't have any more questions, and so this is our last hearing together. We so appreciate your services and really look forward to working with you again in the future, because that's what we do in this work. Thank you.
Thank you for your support.

Thank you to your team. Thank you, guys, for the work that you do. And from this, it seems like we still have a lot of work to do around addressing these racial disparities, and this will be something that's at the top of my priorities to continue to get these numbers down and work with you guys to see how this works, because it seems like there's a lot of things in play, but sometimes this moves a little short, but I only got four years, so we're going to have to move a little bit faster, so thank you guys for the work that you do.
Thank you.
Thank you.
(INAUDIBLE) ACS I know it's not important for you guys to stay and hear (INAUDIBLE)

They actually do stay, because you'll see them, they'll be in the front, so they typically stay in the front. I know, but I'm telling you… well, you're not supposed to make noise in the room, but ACS actually do stay in the room, and they actually stay at all of the hearings. They'll be right here in the front listening. Stephanie, who is actually going to be staying here and moving forward, is here to listen, who has been at all of my hearings to the end, and typically the lone survivor with me at, and so, I just want to make sure that it is known they're not leaving. She's sitting here right in the room, and she does a lot of good work, so. I now open the hearing for public testimony. I remind publics that this is a formal government proceeding, and that decorum shall be always observed. As such, a member of the public shall remain silent at all times. The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify. No radio recordings or photographs allowed at the witness table. Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings at testimony, but you should submit

transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant-at-Arms at the conclusion of the hearing. If you wish to speak today, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant-at-Arms and wait to be recognized. When recognized, you have two minutes to speak today on today's hearing topic, Examining Racial Disparities in the Child Welfare System. If you have a written statement or additional testimony you want to submit for the record, please provide a copy to the Sergeant-at-Arms. I will now call the first panel. You can call them.
Nora McCarthy, Joyce McMillan, and Shalonda Curtis-Hackett.
Did she have testimony you wanted to read for her, or are you?
We'll send it in after.
Okay, no problem. Thank you.
You want to go?
No. Go ahead.
No. You go.

Thank you for the opportunity to testify about the steps that New York City and ACS can take to address racial disparities in how Black and Latinx families are treated by the child welfare system. First, I want to speak about Miranda. ACS is investigating and separating thousands of families every year but keeping them in the dark about their rights. Families are facing the high risk of permanent separation and need Miranda protections. When the government exercises its power to investigate families, parents must be clearly advised orally and in writing in their primary language of their right to remain silent and their right to have an attorney. Second, I want to talk about the Office of Family Well-Being. CAPTA, the Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act, is a federal law that established the core functions of the Child Protection Agency. These are clear and limited. To investigate allegations and to take legal action when children are in danger. Let's be clear, those are policing functions. We must be honest about what ACS

is and what it is not and what it is actually responsible to be. ACS is not a social services agency. It is an investigative and a prosecutorial agency, and so ACS is not the appropriate container or home for providing social support services and resources like family enrichment centers, child care vouchers, and all the other things they seek to do. Social support services and policing are different functions and those functions are governed by different principles. And right now, we are conflating these two functions and it's very dangerous. Parents understand this and, rightfully so, don't trust ACS. If we want ACS (TIMER CHIME) to function properly within the law, we must realign it with its core mandate and strip it of its social service add-ons. This does not mean families should not receive support. Families should receive support from community support. Narrowing the Front Door and the Coalition co-chair recommends the City create new office of family well-being to support community-led planning that supports families, builds up the community supports, and reduces the risk of child welfare involvement.
Thank you.

Hi. Thank you so much. Good afternoon. I'm Nora McCarthy, Director of the New York City Family Policy Project and member of the Narrowing the Front Door work group. Thank you for your attention to the issue of racial disparities and child welfare involvement. I want to add to Joyce's testimony about how we can, thank you, invest in a new approach so that fewer Black and Latino families in particular end up facing crises and ACS involvement. As you know, the Narrowing group and the innovation team and the Mayor's Office of Policy and Planning have been planning a new approach to create an office of family well-being that would anchor a community approach to family support. Thank you for your questions and comments about it earlier. We heard the Commissioner's support. This fall, our group spent time listening to what parents say they need. Parents who rely on City programs and services report needing navigation support that is cross-agency, supportive, and peer-centered. The barriers they named included mistrust, stigma and shame, fear of judgment and consequences including ACS involvement, and resource and time scarcity. The solutions they named included

trusted messengers, peer-based models, neighborhood proximity and proactive outreach, and word of mouth is how parents say they learn about resources through the people and organizations they trust, as you know. A neighborhood strategy that invests in grassroots organizations and the social fabric can ensure that families find the support they need and that crises don't build. A new City office of family well-being can centralize and support family supportive programming, support community-led planning, create new restorative approaches to family safety that prevent and de-escalate family crises, build up networks of peer support to improve access to existing services and resources, and prioritize investment in capacity building in grassroots organizations that families trust. Moreover, we can invest millions in City savings from reductions in ACS spending from the drops that we heard about today. I want to invite all of you on this Committee to a legislative breakfast next month to learn more, and we hope that this Committee and your champions (TIMER CHIME) on the Council more broadly will champion this plan for families. Thanks.

Thank you so much. Yeah. I spoke to someone yesterday about the legislative breakfast. I believe it was (INAUDIBLE) but yes, I look forward to hearing more about that in the upcoming future. I do not have any questions for this panel, and thank you for submitting your questions for today's hearing.
Thank you. It was a pleasure.
Thank you so much. We're going to call the next panel.
The next panel will be Jesse McGleughlin, Fanta-Marie Johnson, and Jasiyah Gilbert.

Thank you. Good afternoon. My name is Fanta-Marie Johnson, and I'm here to talk about the Family Miranda Rights. Thank you to the Chair and the Council for conveying this hearing on providing Family Miranda Rights and racial disparities in New York City's family policing system, sometimes referred to as the child welfare system. My name is Fanta-Marie Johnson, and I am an impacted parent. I am here today to speak about the

harm the family policing system has caused to me and my children, and to call for the passage of the City Family Miranda. When my second son was born in December of 2019, we were drug tested at the hospital without my consent. When we tested positive for cocaine, the hospital reported me to ACS. I was unable to bring my little baby, who looked like the cutest old man who I named Papa, home from the hospital. When ACS came to my home, that's when my life changed forever. The caseworker did not tell me my rights, nor told me that I had the right to a lawyer. We need Family Miranda because parents like me deserve to know our rights when an investigation begins. Had I been informed of my rights and received supportive services early, my son would still be in my care. At every stage of my case, like so many other Black and Latin parents, ACS responses should have been better. I should have been asked, what can we do to support you. Pregnant women go through so much. I should not have to be feared or to fear to tell my truth to my healthcare professionals and ACS caseworkers for fear that my son should be taken out of my care. This system punishes Black families. I went to a Mother and Baby Me program and tested

negative for drugs and alcohol (TIMER CHIME) for the 13 months. While I was there, I received glowing reports from my service providers, yet my son was not placed in my care. Later, my third son was removed from my care after an individual, likely my husband, who had previously committed domestic violence against me, made a false report and manipulated me in the system. This time, I tested negative for all drugs and alcohol, but my son was not placed in my care. I've been sober for years. I finally have overnight visits with my third son, but it should have not taken this long. My sons should have never been removed from my care. I'm fighting for my children, but I am not supported. I'm being punished. This system keeps Black babies and Brown babies in the system to make money. What am I supposed to tell my sons when they grow up? I'm scared.
You can take your time. I'm not going to cut you off, but everybody else, you will be cut off, but you can take your time.

Thank you. I'm scared they're going to become statistics. I'm their mother. I deserve to parent them. They deserve to be

parented by me. I call on the City Council to pass the City Family Miranda and to end the practice of surveilling and separating Black and Latina families.
Thank you for sharing. We really appreciate it.

Thank you for convening this hearing. My name is Jesse McGleughlin, and I'm a Staff Attorney at the Bronx Defenders and a steering committee member of the New York Informed Consent Coalition. I work with Fanta-Marie on that coalition. Our coalition includes people impacted by the family regulation system, along with organizers, activists, doulas, physicians, nurses, social workers, public defenders, and civil rights and reproductive justice organizations. We support policies that improve prenatal care and birth outcomes and that prevent family separation. One of those policies is the Maternal Health Dignity and Consent Act, which would ensure consistent statewide application of clinical best practices by requiring informed consent before drug testing or screening a pregnant or postpartum patient or their newborn unless an emergency situation requires otherwise. I'm here to speak about the harms caused by the test and

report practices in New York City hospitals, which lead to family separation. This practice disproportionately impacts Black and Latina families who are reported to ACS often when there's a positive drug test. We urge the Council to invest in non-punitive and affirming care for pregnant and postpartum people with substance use disorders so that hospitals are places of care, not sites of surveillance. And we know that this works. Nora, who was on the panel earlier from the New York City Family Policy Project, has analyzed ACS data from 2020 to 2024, and that data shows that in 2020, when New York City Health and Hospitals began requiring providers to obtain informed consent before administering a toxicology test on a pregnant patient, an 80 percent drop in ACS investigations alleging parental drug use for mothers of newborns and a 90 percent drop for Black birthing people took place, a 37 percent drop in newborns removed by ACS for any reason, which meant that more newborns stayed at home with their families (TIMER CHIME) and the data did not show that any negative impact…
Ten seconds.
On child safety from the reduced number of ACS investigations. So, these results show that care, not punishment, is the path that we should be taking to support families. Thank you.
Thank you.

My name is Jasiyah Gilbert. Good afternoon. I'm the Client and Community Engagement Manager for the Legal Aid Society's Juvenile Rights Practice, and I'm here both as a professional working in the child welfare space and as someone who was once the subject child of an ACS investigation. When people hear the phrase child protective investigation, they often imagine help arriving at a family's door. But for many families, especially Black and Latino families, it feels far more like an interrogation. As a child, I watched the adults around me panic when ACS showed up, not because there was abuse, but because no one explained their rights. They didn't know what they could refuse. They didn't know when they could ask for a lawyer. They didn't know that saying yes to everything out of fear could permanently change their

lives. By the time legal representation entered the picture, the damage was already done. That was my experience as a child, and it is an experience far too many families in this city know all too well. Children are removed. Families are fractured. Trauma sets in. In the criminal legal system, we understand a basic truth. Rights only matter if people know they have them. That's why Miranda warnings exist. But in the family policing system, where the consequences include family separation and lifelong trauma, parents are rarely informed of their rights at the outset. Instead, they are asked to open their homes, surrender private information, and make life-altering decisions under fear and confusion. Intro. 449 is not about stopping investigations. It's about preventing unnecessary harm before the system starts grinding families down. If parents are informed of their rights early, before court involvement, before removals, families have a real chance to protect themselves and to ask for help. Because once a case enters family court, once children are removed, once trauma compounds, no service, no therapy, and no court order can undo that harm. As someone who lived through an ACS investigation as a child, I can say

this plainly. Miranda-style notice for parents is not radical. It's humane. It's preventative. And it's long overdue. We'll also be submitting written testimony that further expands on these points. If the goal of this system…
Thank you. I don't have any questions for this panel. Thank you for your support on this legislation, and I look forward to continue working with you guys to get this passed. Thank you.

The Commissioner stated ACS opposes Intro. 449, which simply requires ACS to verbally inform parents of their rights to not consent to a search of their home or to force their child to speak to ACS and that they have a right to an attorney. Consider two examples of Bronx Defenders clients' experiences from our 2025 report, This Wound is Still Fresh. ACS does not file a case for five days, refuses to allow the mother to see her child the entire time. A case is filed in court on Wednesday, Bronx Defenders

is assigned, and the family is quickly reunified after a week of family separation. In Thursday, 2023, a similar situation happens where a Latino father is told at his door that he must leave his home by ACS. He is informed court is not going to be held on Monday, but it is in fact held, and by the time (TIMER CHIME) he finally gets to court, it takes a week for him to be reunited with his family. The only thing that can be immediately done to prevent this from happening is to inform parents of their rights, so I ask the Council to pass Intro. 449 and 466 immediately. Thank you.
Thank you.

I'm Jenna Lauter, a Policy Counsel at the New York Civil Liberties Union. The NYCLU views family regulation as a core civil liberties issue that directly implicates the constitutional rights to equal protection, privacy, and family integrity, and undermines the promise of reproductive and racial justice. The family regulation system almost exclusively targets Black and Brown families. This is by design. It was created as backlash to the civil rights movement, a tool to punish Black poverty, and stems from our country's

legacy of devaluing Black motherhood. It also reflects a culture within ACS as described by their own staff that views Black families as inherently less fit and more suspect. Racial disparities deepen as a family regulation case progresses. This means that families of color are not only more likely to be reported, but also more likely to be treated as incompetent or blameworthy and suffer the most severe outcomes. ACS is fundamentally an investigatory and prosecutorial agency that puts families under a microscope and can have a profoundly destabilizing, devastating effect on their lives. Investigations and family separations inflict stress and trauma that do more to harm than to help children's well-being. The data bears this out. This punitive approach is especially unwarranted given that over 75 percent of ACS cases stem from circumstances related to poverty, not intentional maltreatment. These are loving, caring families that are being ripped apart. To genuinely improve child welfare, the City should immediately enact Intros 0449 and 0466 to ensure parents know their constitutional rights when government agents come to their door. Parents must be told their rights verbally in real time so they can

make informed decisions in high-stakes moments. The City should also invest in programs like universal childcare, affordable housing, and cash assistance to help families break intergenerational cycles of poverty and trauma and truly thrive. ACS just acknowledged that parents fear engaging in services provided by an agency with the power to take their children away. This includes the CARES program. The City should disentangle resource provision from ACS and ensure that all families can freely access supportive (TIMER CHIME) programs with zero ACS involvement. Thank you.
Thank you.

Should this Committee want to move our city beyond naming these harms and bring us to a place of action to empower and support families, it must continue to move this legislation forward. Intro. 449 ensures that agents of ACS retain all existing legal authority to conduct investigations while verbally providing parents with the information and transparency they need to protect their families from any unlawful abuse of that

authority. This is straightforward legislation, and it doesn't create any new rights. Ensuring that parents have knowledge of their existing rights during an ACS investigation will allow parents to make informed decisions for their family and minimize the harm of confusion of ACS investigation. Like in all other parts of life, better informed parents can make better decisions for their children. Given the current escalation in government surveillance and the increased fear of family separation amongst our city's most marginalized communities, it is vital that we immediately take action to protect family integrity. The last thing I'll note (TIMER CHIME) is we ask that Introduction 466 be amended to include the full provision of rights that's listed in 449 so that two bills parallel each other. Thank you. Thank you for your support of the bill. We're working through it in my hopes to get it passed, so thank you and continue to work with you guys on your advocacy so we can get it passed. Thank you.

Partnership. A copy of the presentation is included. ACS will fund this over three years to financially support an expanded Nurse-Family Partnership Program.
